rv.q: The play is a masterpiece of theatrical construction, and this revival does it full justice.
The production, directed by Rebecca Taichman, captures both the buoyancy of youth and the melancholy of middle age with equal facility.

Priestley is not always subtle in pointing out how precisely things have gone wrong for the characters; some ironies seem to land like bricks, and while the fog of disillusion is convincing, we in the 21st century cannot be expected to find all his revelations to be, well, revelatory.
Time and the Conways is a funny old play, interesting more for its structural adventurousness than its thematic trenchancy.
Though the Roundabout production, which opened on Tuesday evening, stars Elizabeth McGovern as the materfamilias, the story really is Kay’s.
It’s a great scene, but first we have to get there, and the erratic directorial style makes that rougher than it needs to be.
Time and the Conways rarely pulled me in.
But Time and the Conways requires a stronger gravitational force than McGovern’s airy performance provides.
While Chekhov’s critique of bourgeois blindness was never stuck in 1904, Time and the Conways might be pretty thoroughly trapped in 1937.
Time and the Conways should be equally unnerving, but here it’s simply undone.
As deftly handled by director Rebecca Taichman (a 2017. Tony winner for Indecent), Priestley’s metaphysics are poignant where, in less able hands, they could come off as annoyingly mystical.
Sometimes you do walk out humming the scenery.

It's hard to like or care about the characters, who exist in two fundamentally off-putting registers: When they are up, they are rah-rah party kittens playing charades, and when they are down they are grizzly and miserable.
If it’s an “interesting enough” time you’re looking for.
All in all this is a bland production of an earnest philosophy.
Except for a handful of striking moments, the play comes off as a boring mishmash of Chekhov’s “The Cherry Orchard,” Sondheim’s “Merrily Along” and, of course, “Downton Abbey.”
When emotions run high, the shouty and overly declarative acting can overwhelm the small stage.
It‘s the kind of plot that could be a soap opera or high-concept TV serial, if the writing wasn’t so subtle, the characters so good and director Rebecca Taichman so focused and sharp.

cn.t: Critics find Priestley's 1937 drama an intriguing but dated period piece whose philosophical concepts about time prove more compelling than the drama itself. The handsome production and strong performances can't fully overcome stilted dialogue and uneven pacing.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
